subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Hot Jupiters
description: A quick win: understand Hot Jupiters.

hook.text: Hot Jupiters are gas giants that orbit insanely close to their stars—some completing a year in less than two days.

buildup.text: Their surface temperatures can reach 2,000°C. Some are so hot that iron and glass rain down from their clouds.

discovery.text: 51 Pegasi b was the first found—a Jupiter-mass planet orbiting its star in just 4.2 days. It shocked astronomers.

twist.text: They can't form where they are now. They must have migrated inward from farther out, rewriting planetary formation theory.

climax.text: Some are tidally locked—one side always faces the star. The day side roasts while the night side is far cooler.

punchline.text: Jupiter-sized, furnace-hot, impossibly close. Worlds that shouldn't be where they are.

quiz.question: Why do hot Jupiters challenge planetary formation theory?
options: They can't form so close to a star and must have migrated inward
They are too massive to have formed from a protoplanetary disk
Their atmospheres contain elements not found in gas giant models

details.summary: Hot Jupiters are gas giant exoplanets that orbit extremely close to their host stars — often completing an orbit in just a few days. With surface temperatures exceeding 1,000°C, they were the first type of exoplanet discovered and challenged existing planet formation theories, which couldn't…
details.whyItMatters: Hot Jupiters forced astronomers to rethink planetary formation and migration. Their existence proved that planetary systems can be radically different from our own solar system.
takeaways: Gas giants orbiting extremely close to their host stars
Surface temperatures exceed 1,000°C with orbits of just days
Their discovery challenged planet formation theories

faq.question: How did hot Jupiters form so close to their stars?
faq.answer: They didn't form there. Gas giants need cold conditions to accumulate hydrogen and helium, available only far from the star. faq.question: Are hot Jupiters common?
faq.answer: Surprisingly rare — only about 1% of Sun-like stars host one. They were the first exoplanets found because they're the easiest to detect (large planets with short periods produce the strongest signals).
